sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Explain the difference between a population distribution and the sampling distribution of a sample mean \(\bar{x}\).
questions.target: What is a sampling distribution?
questions.answer: The population distribution describes the values of individual members of the entire population. The sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) describes the values that the sample mean would take if you repeatedly took many samples of the same size from that population and computed the mean of each sample — it describes variability between different samples' means, not between individuals.
questions.explanation: The population distribution describes the values of individual members of the entire population. The sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) describes the values that the sample mean would take if you repeatedly took many samples of the same size from that population and computed the mean of each sample — it describes variability between different samples' means, not between individuals.

questions.q: Explain why the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) has less variability than the original population distribution.
questions.target: What is a sampling distribution?
questions.answer: A sample mean averages together multiple individual values, and averaging tends to smooth out extreme individual values — some will be higher and some lower than the true mean, partially canceling out. This averaging effect makes sample means cluster more tightly around the population mean than individual values do.
questions.explanation: A sample mean averages together multiple individual values, and averaging tends to smooth out extreme individual values — some will be higher and some lower than the true mean, partially canceling out. This averaging effect makes sample means cluster more tightly around the population mean than individual values do.

questions.q: A population has mean \(\mu=60\) and standard deviation \(\sigma=12\). For samples of size \(n=36\), find the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\).
questions.target: Mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution
questions.answer: Mean of \(\bar{x}\): \(\mu_{\bar{x}}=\mu=60\) (unbiased — the sampling distribution's mean equals the population mean). Standard deviation of \(\bar{x}\) (standard error): \(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=\frac{12}{6}=2\).
questions.explanation: Mean of \(\bar{x}\): \(\mu_{\bar{x}}=\mu=60\) (unbiased — the sampling distribution's mean equals the population mean). Standard deviation of \(\bar{x}\) (standard error): \(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=\frac{12}{6}=2\).

questions.q: Using the same population, find the standard error for a larger sample of size \(n=144\), and explain what happens to the standard error as sample size increases.
questions.target: Mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution
questions.answer: \(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{144}}=\frac{12}{12}=1\). As sample size increases, the standard error decreases (specifically, it decreases proportionally to \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\)) — larger samples give more precise (less variable) estimates of the population mean.
questions.explanation: \(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{12}{\sqrt{144}}=\frac{12}{12}=1\). As sample size increases, the standard error decreases (specifically, it decreases proportionally to \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\)) — larger samples give more precise (less variable) estimates of the population mean.

questions.q: State the Central Limit Theorem in your own words, including what happens to the shape of the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) as sample size \(n\) increases.
questions.target: The Central Limit Theorem
questions.answer: The Central Limit Theorem states that as sample size \(n\) increases, the sampling distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) becomes approximately normal, regardless of the shape of the original population distribution — even if the population itself is skewed or unusual in shape. A commonly used guideline is that \(n\geq30\) is generally large enough for this approximation to be reasonable.
questions.explanation: The Central Limit Theorem states that as sample size \(n\) increases, the sampling distribution of the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) becomes approximately normal, regardless of the shape of the original population distribution — even if the population itself is skewed or unusual in shape. A commonly used guideline is that \(n\geq30\) is generally large enough for this approximation to be reasonable.

questions.q: Explain why the Central Limit Theorem is considered one of the most important results in statistics, referencing its practical usefulness.
questions.target: The Central Limit Theorem
questions.answer: The Central Limit Theorem is powerful because it allows statisticians to use normal-distribution-based methods (like \(z\)-scores and confidence intervals) for the sample mean even when the underlying population distribution is unknown or clearly not normal — as long as the sample size is reasonably large, this makes a huge range of inference procedures broadly applicable.
questions.explanation: The Central Limit Theorem is powerful because it allows statisticians to use normal-distribution-based methods (like \(z\)-scores and confidence intervals) for the sample mean even when the underlying population distribution is unknown or clearly not normal — as long as the sample size is reasonably large, this makes a huge range of inference procedures broadly applicable.

questions.q: Starting from \(P(A \cap B) = 0.07\) and \(P(B) = 0.35\), find \(P(A \mid B)\).
questions.answer: **Answer:** D. \(P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\dfrac{0.07}{0.35}=0.2\).

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: A population has a true proportion \(p=0.4\) favoring a proposal. For samples of size \(n=100\), find the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the sample proportion \(\hat{p}\), using \(\sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\).
questions.target: Sampling distribution of a sample proportion
questions.answer: Mean: \(\mu_{\hat{p}}=p=0.4\). Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.4(0.6)}{100}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.24}{100}}=\sqrt{0.0024}\approx0.049\).
questions.explanation: Mean: \(\mu_{\hat{p}}=p=0.4\). Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.4(0.6)}{100}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.24}{100}}=\sqrt{0.0024}\approx0.049\).

questions.q: State the two conditions typically required to treat the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) as approximately normal.
questions.target: Sampling distribution of a sample proportion
questions.answer: Both \(np\geq10\) and \(n(1-p)\geq10\) must hold (sometimes stated as needing at least 10 expected successes and 10 expected failures) — this ensures the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is not too skewed to approximate with a normal curve.
questions.explanation: Both \(np\geq10\) and \(n(1-p)\geq10\) must hold (sometimes stated as needing at least 10 expected successes and 10 expected failures) — this ensures the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) is not too skewed to approximate with a normal curve.

questions.q: Explain, in the context of opinion polling, why a poll of 1000 people gives a more reliable estimate of a population proportion than a poll of 50 people, connecting your answer to the formula for \(\sigma_{\hat{p}}\).
questions.target: Comparing sampling variability across sample sizes
questions.answer: Since \(\sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\) decreases as \(n\) increases, a larger sample size produces a smaller standard error for the sample proportion — meaning the sample proportion from a poll of 1000 people tends to land closer to the true population proportion, on average, than a poll of only 50 people, which is subject to much more sample-to-sample variability.
questions.explanation: Since \(\sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\) decreases as \(n\) increases, a larger sample size produces a smaller standard error for the sample proportion — meaning the sample proportion from a poll of 1000 people tends to land closer to the true population proportion, on average, than a poll of only 50 people, which is subject to much more sample-to-sample variability.

questions.q: Knowing that \(P(A \cap B) = 0.25\) and \(P(B) = 0.38\), find \(P(A \mid B)\).
questions.answer: **Answer:** B. \(P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\dfrac{0.25}{0.38}=0.6579\).

questions.q: A population of insurance claim amounts is strongly right-skewed. Explain why a sample of size \(n=15\) might not be large enough to safely use CLT-based normal methods, but a sample of size \(n=200\) likely would be.
questions.target: Sample size and the CLT threshold
questions.answer: The Central Limit Theorem's normal approximation improves as sample size increases, and it takes a larger sample size to overcome a strongly skewed population shape. With only \(n=15\), the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) may still noticeably reflect the skewness of the original population, making normal-based methods unreliable. With \(n=200\) (well beyond the common \(n\geq30\) guideline), the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) is much more likely to be close to normal, even though the original population itself is skewed.
questions.explanation: The Central Limit Theorem's normal approximation improves as sample size increases, and it takes a larger sample size to overcome a strongly skewed population shape. With only \(n=15\), the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) may still noticeably reflect the skewness of the original population, making normal-based methods unreliable. With \(n=200\) (well beyond the common \(n\geq30\) guideline), the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) is much more likely to be close to normal, even though the original population itself is skewed.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the standard deviation of an individual population value and the standard error of a sample mean \(\bar{x}\).
questions.target: Standard error vs. standard deviation
questions.answer: The standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) measures the spread of individual values within the population. The standard error (\(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)) measures the spread of sample means across many hypothetical samples of the same size — it is always smaller than \(\sigma\) (for \(n>1\)), since averaging reduces variability.
questions.explanation: The standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) measures the spread of individual values within the population. The standard error (\(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)) measures the spread of sample means across many hypothetical samples of the same size — it is always smaller than \(\sigma\) (for \(n>1\)), since averaging reduces variability.

questions.q: A quality control engineer at a bottling plant knows that individual bottle fill volumes are approximately normal with mean \(500\) mL and standard deviation \(8\) mL. Every hour, the engineer measures a sample of 16 bottles and computes the sample mean fill volume. Describe the shape, mean, and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of this hourly sample mean, and explain whether the Central Limit Theorem's usual \(n\geq30\) guideline is even needed to justify treating this sampling distribution as normal.
questions.target: Standard error vs. standard deviation
questions.answer: Shape: approximately normal. Mean: \(\mu_{\bar{x}}=500\) mL (same as the population mean). Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{8}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{8}{4}=2\) mL. The \(n\geq30\) CLT guideline is not needed here, because the underlying population of individual fill volumes is already stated to be approximately normal — when the population itself is normal, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) is exactly normal for any sample size, including small ones like \(n=16\).
questions.explanation: Shape: approximately normal. Mean: \(\mu_{\bar{x}}=500\) mL (same as the population mean). Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{8}{\sqrt{16}}=\frac{8}{4}=2\) mL. The \(n\geq30\) CLT guideline is not needed here, because the underlying population of individual fill volumes is already stated to be approximately normal — when the population itself is normal, the sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) is exactly normal for any sample size, including small ones like \(n=16\).

questions.q: A political pollster samples 900 voters and calculates a sample proportion \(\hat{p}=0.53\) supporting a ballot measure, from a true population proportion of \(p=0.50\). Verify that both conditions (\(np\geq10\) and \(n(1-p)\geq10\)) are satisfied for treating the sampling distribution of \(\hat{p}\) as approximately normal, then find the standard deviation of this sampling distribution, to four decimal places.
questions.target: Standard error vs. standard deviation
questions.answer: \(np=900(0.50)=450\geq10\) ✓. \(n(1-p)=900(0.50)=450\geq10\) ✓. Both conditions are satisfied. Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}=\sqrt{\frac{(0.50)(0.50)}{900}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.25}{900}}\approx0.0167\).
questions.explanation: \(np=900(0.50)=450\geq10\) ✓. \(n(1-p)=900(0.50)=450\geq10\) ✓. Both conditions are satisfied. Standard deviation: \(\sigma_{\hat{p}}=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}=\sqrt{\frac{(0.50)(0.50)}{900}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.25}{900}}\approx0.0167\).

questions.q: A large factory produces light bulbs whose individual lifespans are strongly right-skewed (most bulbs fail early, but a few last an unusually long time), with population mean \(\mu=800\) hours and standard deviation \(\sigma=250\) hours. An engineer takes a random sample of \(n=64\) bulbs and computes the sample mean lifespan. Explain, step by step, why it is reasonable to treat this sampling distribution of \(\bar{x}\) as approximately normal despite the population itself being skewed, then compute the standard error of \(\bar{x}\).
questions.target: Standard error vs. standard deviation
questions.answer: Even though the individual bulb lifespans are strongly skewed, the Central Limit Theorem states that the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal as sample size increases, regardless of the population's original shape. Since \(n=64\) comfortably exceeds the common guideline of \(n\geq30\), it is reasonable to treat \(\bar{x}\)'s sampling distribution as approximately normal here. Standard error: \(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{250}{\sqrt{64}}=\frac{250}{8}=31.25\) hours.
questions.explanation: Even though the individual bulb lifespans are strongly skewed, the Central Limit Theorem states that the sampling distribution of the sample mean becomes approximately normal as sample size increases, regardless of the population's original shape. Since \(n=64\) comfortably exceeds the common guideline of \(n\geq30\), it is reasonable to treat \(\bar{x}\)'s sampling distribution as approximately normal here. Standard error: \(\sigma_{\bar{x}}=\frac{250}{\sqrt{64}}=\frac{250}{8}=31.25\) hours.

questions.answer: **Answer:** B. \(P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\dfrac{0.12}{0.24}=0.5\).

questions.q: Level 2 · MediumExplain the difference between a single-blind experiment and a double-blind experiment, and describe why a placebo is used in medical trials.
questions.target: Standard error vs. standard deviation
questions.answer: Single-Blind: Either the subjects do not know which treatment they are receiving, OR the evaluators who measure the response do not know which treatment was administered. Double-Blind: NEITHER the subjects nor the researchers/evaluators interacting with them and measuring response variables know which treatment was administered. Placebo Purpose: A placebo provides an inactive comparison baseline that isolates the physiological effect of the active medication from psychological improvements caused simply by receiving treatment (the placebo effect).
questions.explanation: Single-Blind: Either the subjects do not know which treatment they are receiving, OR the evaluators who measure the response do not know which treatment was administered. Double-Blind: NEITHER the subjects nor the researchers/evaluators interacting with them and measuring response variables know which treatment was administered. Placebo Purpose: A placebo provides an inactive comparison baseline that isolates the physiological effect of the active medication from psychological improvements caused simply by receiving treatment (the placebo effect).

questions.q: Level 3 · AdvancedTen athletes participate in a vertical jump training program. Their jump heights (in inches) before and after the program are recorded. To test whether the program increased jump height, explain why a paired t-test is appropriate rather than a two-sample t-test, state the null and alternative hypotheses, and specify the degrees of freedom.
questions.target: What is a sampling distribution?
questions.answer: Why Paired: The observations are paired on the same subjects (before and after measurements on each athlete). The two samples are dependent, not independent. Hypotheses: Letting \(\mu_d = \mu_{\mathrm{after}} - \mu_{\mathrm{before}}\) be the true mean difference in jump height: \(H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad \mathrm{vs.} \quad H_a: \mu_d > 0.\) Degrees of Freedom: Since this is a one-sample test on differences: \(df = n - 1 = 10 - 1 = \mathbf{9}.\)
questions.explanation: Why Paired: The observations are paired on the same subjects (before and after measurements on each athlete). The two samples are dependent, not independent. Hypotheses: Letting \(\mu_d = \mu_{\mathrm{after}} - \mu_{\mathrm{before}}\) be the true mean difference in jump height: \(H_0: \mu_d = 0 \quad \mathrm{vs.} \quad H_a: \mu_d > 0.\) Degrees of Freedom: Since this is a one-sample test on differences: \(df = n - 1 = 10 - 1 = \mathbf{9}.\)

A quality control process monitors the weight, \(W\) grams, of chocolate bars produced by a machine. A random sample of 50 chocolate bars was taken, and their weights were recorded. The sample mean weight was 102.5 grams, and the sample standard deviation was 3.5 grams. A) Calculate the standard error of the mean. B) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight of the chocolate bars. C) The machine is calibrated to produce chocolate bars with a mean weight of \(\mu_0 = 100\) grams. Based on your confidence interval, what conclusion can be drawn about the calibration of the machine?
questions.target: Mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution
choices: The machine is likely calibrated correctly, as \(\mu_0\) is within the interval.
The machine is likely not calibrated correctly, as \(\mu_0\) is outside the interval.
The machine is likely calibrated correctly, as the sample mean is close to \(\mu_0\).
The machine is likely not calibrated correctly, as the sample standard deviation is too large.
questions.answer: A) The standard error of the mean (SE) is calculated using the formula: \(SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\), where \(s\) is the sample standard deviation and \(n\) is the sample size. Given \(s = 3.5\) grams and \(n = 50\). \(SE = \frac{3.5}{\sqrt{50}} \approx \frac{3.5}{7.071} \approx 0.495\) grams. B) To construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight, we use the formula: \(CI = \bar{x} \pm z^* \times SE\), where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean and \(z^*\) is the critical z-value for a 95% confidence level. For a 95% confidence level, \(z^* \approx 1.96\). Given \(\bar{x} = 102.5\) grams and \(SE \approx 0.495\) grams. \(CI = 102.5 \pm 1.96 \times 0.495\) \(CI = 102.5 \pm 0.9702\) The 95% confidence interval is approximately \((101.53, 103.47)\) grams. C) The machine is calibrated to produce chocolate bars with a mean weight of \(\mu_0 = 100\) grams. Our calculated 95% confidence interval for the mean weight is \((101.53, 103.47)\) grams. Since the hypothesized mean weight of 100 grams lies outside this interval, we have statistically significant evidence to conclude that the machine is likely not calibrated correctly to produce chocolate bars with a mean weight of 100 grams.
questions.explanation: A) The standard error of the mean (SE) is calculated using the formula: \(SE = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\), where \(s\) is the sample standard deviation and \(n\) is the sample size. Given \(s = 3.5\) grams and \(n = 50\). \(SE = \frac{3.5}{\sqrt{50}} \approx \frac{3.5}{7.071} \approx 0.495\) grams. B) To construct a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight, we use the formula: \(CI = \bar{x} \pm z^* \times SE\), where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean and \(z^*\) is the critical z-value for a 95% confidence level. For a 95% confidence level, \(z^* \approx 1.96\). Given \(\bar{x} = 102.5\) grams and \(SE \approx 0.495\) grams. \(CI = 102.5 \pm 1.96 \times 0.495\) \(CI = 102.5 \pm 0.9702\) The 95% confidence interval is approximately \((101.53, 103.47)\) grams. C) The machine is calibrated to produce chocolate bars with a mean weight of \(\mu_0 = 100\) grams. Our calculated 95% confidence interval for the mean weight is \((101.53, 103.47)\) grams. Since the hypothesized mean weight of 100 grams lies outside this interval, we have statistically significant evidence to conclude that the machine is likely not calibrated correctly to produce chocolate bars with a mean weight of 100 grams.

questions.q: A researcher wants to estimate a population proportion with a margin of error of at most \(\pm 2\%\) at a 95% confidence level. An earlier study with \(n = 400\) had a margin of error of \(\pm 5\%\). Approximately what sample size \(n\) is required?
questions.target: The Central Limit Theorem
questions.answer: \(\mathrm{MOE} \propto 1/\sqrt{n} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{MOE}_1}{\mathrm{MOE}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{n_2}{n_1}} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{n_2}{400}} \Rightarrow 2.5^2 = \frac{n_2}{400} \Rightarrow 6.25 \times 400 = 2,500\).
questions.explanation: \(\mathrm{MOE} \propto 1/\sqrt{n} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{MOE}_1}{\mathrm{MOE}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{n_2}{n_1}} \Rightarrow \frac{5}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{n_2}{400}} \Rightarrow 2.5^2 = \frac{n_2}{400} \Rightarrow 6.25 \times 400 = 2,500\).

questions.target: Applying the Central Limit Theorem
choices: Mean = \(3\mu - 5\), SD = \(3\sigma - 5\)
Mean = \(3\mu - 5\), SD = \(3\sigma\)
